extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, creative writers, and literary-minded readers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for poets and imaginative writers on cultivating and expressing imagination, using symbols, achieving universality, and the personal sacrifices and methods required for poetic creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination and tropes as liberation
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of symbols has a certain power of emancipation and exhilaration for all men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tropes, fables, oracles, and all poetic forms excite a metamorphosis in the reader that liberates imagination and imparts joy. Examples: Aristotle's and Plato's metaphors, Vitruvius's remark linking anatomy and architecture, Chaucer's similes, Aesop's animal masquerades, John's Apocalypse as imagery. The criterion values the power of symbolic metamorphosis to open new senses and worlds for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of the transcendental and extraordinary in books
rubrics_metrics.description: I think nothing is of any value in books excepting the transcendental and extraordinary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize the imaginative, visionary, and extraordinary elements in writing; the mere accumulation of arguments, histories, and criticism is secondary. Writers who are 'inflamed' and carried away by a single dream or vision provide the work's chief value, even if they introduce questionable or fantastical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as departure from routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Questionable facts or bold departures (angels, devils, magic, astrology, etc.) serve as a certificate of departure from routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of eccentric or heterodox ideas (as in Pythagoras, Paracelsus, Swedenborg, etc.) signals imaginative liberty and can be a positive marker of originality. The standard rewards works that show a clear departure from conventional, routine thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep symbols fluid; avoid mysticism's fixity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mysticism consists in the mistake of an accidental and individual symbol for an universal one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold symbols lightly; do not nail a personal or accidental symbol as universally true. Translate private symbols into equivalents others use; prefer more universal signs ('a little algebra') to village or idiosyncratic symbols. Anti-pattern: insisting that one private symbol must mean the same to all readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination should flow, not freeze
rubrics_metrics.description: But the quality of the imagination is to flow, and not to freeze.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination must be dynamic and moving; poetic language and symbolism are 'fluxional' and vehicular. Avoid rigid or fixed interpretations and forms that arrest living possibility; allow language and metaphor to change and convey new thought continuously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as liberator/introducer of new thought
rubrics_metrics.description: He unlocks our chains and admits us to a new scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet's work is measured by its ability to emancipate readers from habitual perspective and to introduce genuinely new thoughts and scenes. The poet who grants 'a new sense' or shows another nested world fulfills this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express symmetrically and abundantly (avoid fragmentary work)
rubrics_metrics.description: to express themselves symmetrically and abundantly, not dwarfishly and fragmentarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic expression should aim for fullness and symmetry rather than scant or disjointed utterance. Artists are called to immerse themselves in adequate conditions (subjects, scenes) and to pursue the beauty half seen, producing sustained, abundant work — the great poets have 'no limits' except life and can mirror every created thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and compulsive productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubt not, O poet, but persist. Say 'It is in me, and shall out.'... Stand there, balked and dumb... stand and strive, until at last rage draw out of thee that dream-power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistence in the face of ridicule, silence, or failure is essential. Produce prolifically (accept that much will be conventional) until the genuinely original utterance appears. The standard values stubborn, compulsive creative labor that yields breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willing renunciation of worldly life for the muse
rubrics_metrics.description: Thou shalt leave the world, and know the muse only... Thou shalt pass for a fool and a churl for a long season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for social marginality: seclusion, apprenticeship, and reputational costs are often necessary to sustain the poet's inward life. Others may perform worldly roles while the poet preserves the ideal; this renunciation is presented as a legitimate condition of true poetic vocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local/national materials to create universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Our logrolling, our stumps and their politics, our fisheries, our Negroes and Indians... are yet unsung. Yet America is a poem in our eyes; its ample geography dazzles the imagination, and it will not wait long for metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should 'chaunt our own times and social circumstance' — local, contemporaneous materials can and should be transformed into universal poetry. Cultural particularity, when seized imaginatively, attains universal scope (Dante's autobiographical universality invoked as example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passionate insight outweighs learned argument
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man is inflamed and carried away by his thought... let me read his paper, and you may have all the arguments and histories and criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vital, passionate vision is more valuable than polished, argumentative scholarship. The presence of deep feeling and imaginative conviction in a work is a stronger criterion of merit than exhaustive evidentiary apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceive transformations and multiple aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: The same man or society of men may wear one aspect to themselves and their companions, and a different aspect to higher intelligences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic perception involves seeing things in transformation and recognizing multiple, coexisting aspects (as in Swedenborg's visions and other examples). The poet should reveal these transformations, making strange familiar things and showing alternate aspects of persons and societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive literariness or mere literal historicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton is too literary, and Homer too literal and historical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware two extremes: over-literariness (excessive artifice) and over-literalness (mere historical narrative). The ideal poet balances imaginative universality with form, avoiding being merely 'literary' or merely 'historical.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic methods are ideal and eternal; enter the condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is the path of the creator to his work. The paths or methods are ideal and eternal, though few men ever see them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists must put themselves in the conditions that call them (scenes, assemblies, figures) and respond to the inner beckoning. The method is not merely technique but entering an imaginative condition where daemons and shapes come; authenticity demands immersion rather than formulaic craft alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: First stimulate the reader through tropes; exact sense comes later
rubrics_metrics.description: An imaginative book renders us much more service at first, by stimulating us through its tropes, than afterward when we arrive at the precise sense of the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize initial imaginative impact: the immediate exhilaration and liberation produced by tropes is the primary service of imaginative writing. Precise, didactic sense may follow but should not be the work's chief claim to value.
